image.prompt:
Product photograph of one isolated object, shot from a HIGH THREE-QUARTER ANGLE: the camera is well above the object and tilted down about 30 degrees, so the top of the object is clearly visible along with its front and one side. Not a straight-on elevation.

The object: Standalone single-storey 7-Eleven convenience store building, detailed front elevation with full-width glass frontage and automatic sliding doors under a deep white fascia band carrying the orange green and red horizontal stripe device and the 7-ELEVEN wordmark, backlit lightbox sign and slim canopy edge, interior shelving faintly visible behind the glass, plain rendered side and rear walls with a service door and a small high window, flat roof with a low parapet and roof-mounted air-conditioning condensers Materials: white powder-coated aluminium and plate glass at the front, glossy printed lightbox vinyl, flat painted render on the side and rear walls, galvanised roof plant.

Form: build the object from a few simple, chunky, closed volumes. Prefer solid panels over lattice, mesh, grilles or perforated screens; keep any openings few, large and clearly separated. No thin spindly protrusions, no wires, no chains, no fringes, no lace, no fine filigree, no dense repeated slots or cut-outs. Keep the silhouette simple and readable from every side. Keep the object's SHAPE simple; richness must come from the surface finish, wear and materials rather than from intricate geometry. The object is still photoreal and highly detailed in its texture -- only its form is simple.

Framing: long-lens near-orthographic perspective, minimal foreshortening. The object is perfectly centred and occupies about 75% of the frame height, with clear empty margin on all four sides. The whole object is in frame; nothing is cropped.

Background: completely flat seamless neutral 50% grey (#808080). The object floats in empty space against an infinite seamless backdrop, photographed as a cut-out with nothing underneath it. There is no surface for it to rest on and nothing for it to cast a shadow onto. No floor, no ground plane, no horizon line, no cast shadow, no contact shadow, no reflection, no vignette, no gradient.

Lighting: flat even studio illumination from all sides, soft and shadowless, like a lightbox. No strong key light, no rim light, no coloured light, no specular blowout, no dramatic highlights. Colours must read as true albedo.

One object only, nothing else in frame. No people, no hands, no other props, no packaging, no watermarks, no measurement annotations, no arrows, no borders, no drop shadow. Apart from the building's own signage described above, there is no other text or lettering anywhere in the frame.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, clean and undamaged geometry, realistic materials and surface wear. Not stylised, not cartoon, not low-poly, not a 3D render preview, not a wireframe.

review.critique: Fidelity 0.86 -> 0.90. The baked shopfront interior is gone at the user's direction and the feature that scored it is re-scoped to what an exterior shell can deliver; the rectification stays as the ruler and sized the manifestation row it replaced. Two runtime-contract defects fixed: the sign-mount socket shipped as 'socket-0' with its real name buried in userData, and it was parented to building-shell, whose -pi/2 extrude rotation put the declared local (0, 3.54, 3.5) at world (0, 3.5, -3.54) -- on the back wall. Both corrected against the spec, which was right. Front stack re-solved: wall 4.25 -> 4.40, fascia tray 0.92 -> 1.10, head-to-sign gap 0.22 -> 0.34. Side elevation and shell albedos solved through the face's own measured transfer instead of copied from the plate. Gates: turntable PASS with zero holed pixels at every azimuth, check-coplanar clean at 0.001 m, check_part_coverage 0 errors / 0 warnings, all four budget axes inside hero4x. Silhouette IoU 0.568 still fails its 0.85 threshold and the cause is now measured, not asserted: the harness's fixed 35-degree camera rakes the roofline across 0.146 of the frame where the plate's long lens rakes it across 0.018. interiorDifference moved 0.0558 -> 0.0591 over the whole pass, and that is the honest cost of the front stack: an 8x8 mean-colour grid rewards a correctly-sized sign band landing in the plate's cells, and under a different lens a physically correct band cannot. The physical proportion is the right target for a game prop; the pixel layout of one photograph is not.

featureReviews.notes: Up from 0.86. The front wall was raised 4.25 -> 4.40 m with the coping cap sitting ON it (4.40..4.45) rather than inside its last 50 mm, which is also what took check-coplanar back to clean: a cap whose top face shares the wall's top plane is a same-facing pair over 53 m2. Measured at the solved camera (azimuth 34 / elevation 22, re-confirmed here by an elevation sweep -- silhouette aspect 1.713 at el10, 1.570 at el14, 1.458 at el18, 1.370 at el22 against the plate's 1.320, so el22 is the match and nothing lower is): aspectRatioDelta 0.042 -> 0.0296, scaleDelta 0.0017, silhouette IoU 0.507 -> 0.568. Total height 4.59 m (the condenser), inside the 4.60 m module the fourteen shared-module buildings all use. IoU still fails its 0.85 threshold and the reason is now MEASURED rather than asserted: scanning the first foreground row across the frame, the plate's top edge runs y 0.042..0.060 of the silhouette height -- essentially flat -- while the render's runs 0.164..0.018, eight times the convergence. The harness camera is a fixed 35 degree perspective shared by every prop in the kit and by img2threejs's own gates; the plate is a long-lens product render. That is an instrument difference, it is not changeable for one asset, and it caps IoU here.

Up from 0.85. The manifestation decal row is BUILT, at the height and pitch the rectified opening measures (sign/glass.png at 170.7 px/m: the row occupies pixel rows 223-241, i.e. 1.47 m above grade; dashes 0.14 m wide on a 0.27 m pitch, so 22 across the 6.00 m shopfront). It used to be printed into the baked glazing image, which is why an earlier geometry row was dropped -- it landed at 1.20 m and read as a second row beside the printed one. With the image gone there is one row and it is where the plate puts it. Tones are the plate's own, not the brand palette: its tab pixels measure saturation 0.37-0.49 at luma 114-128 against a pane reading 136, so the three are set at brand hue mixed 45% into the pane tone. At full strength they drew a bold dashed line the plate does not have. The head-to-fascia gap opened 0.22 -> 0.34 m (framing top 2.86, tray bottom 3.20). Four bays, centred pair, framed leaves, kickplate and head as before; the row rides in the existing mullion InstancedMesh's material family and costs one draw call and the spec's already-declared decal-tab material, which nothing had ever instantiated.

Up from 0.86. It was a low SLAB: measured off the plate's own roof crop at the unit's depth, apparent height over apparent width is 0.61 and the 1.30 x 0.60 box rendered 0.46. At 1.15 x 0.68 x 0.95 it renders 0.59, without touching the 4.59 m ceiling. The two fans are RECESSED into the flat lid -- a bright rolled rim, a dark throat, a guard -- drawn in the atlas quadrant, where they were two proud cylinders; that is what the plate shows and it removes two lathe rings, so the fix costs negative triangles. The first cut of the recess put ONE fan the size of the whole lid, which is a different machine; there are two at 0.44 of the lid width each. The unit stands on a dark bearer rail rather than four feet. The duct is ONE run with a standing seam and an end cap, where three flange ribs standing 15 mm proud read as a staircase of separate blocks. The coil louvre is now DARK: it had been lifted to luma 130 to clear the turntable's hole test at the backdrop's 58, and the right lever is chroma, not value -- #35485a is luma 68 at saturation 0.41, below the backdrop and nothing like it in chroma. Placement moved from (2.60, 2.20) to (1.60, -1.20): a three-quarter view of a flat roof pushes anything on it toward the near corner, and the unit was crowding the front-right parapet. RESIDUAL, named: the plate and the Meshy proxy both put the parapet at about 0.89 of total height, so the unit should stand roughly twice as proud of the coping as it does. Closing that needs a 5.0 m total, and this asset is one of fourteen sharing an 8.0 x 4.6 x 7.0 module. The module wins; the shortfall is recorded rather than smoothed over.

Up from 0.84, which had been 'Unchanged' for two passes. The graphic itself was never the problem -- it is the plate's own measured palette and layout with the trademark artwork baked in -- the SIZE was. Column-scanning the coloured stripes in the normalised frame: the plate's band (orange top to red bottom) spans 0.1033 of the silhouette height and the build spanned 0.0783, 24% short. The tray went 0.92 -> 1.10 m and the graphic face 0.80 -> 0.98 m, which takes the band to 0.0950 -- 8% short, and the remainder is what the 4.6 m module leaves between the shopfront head and the coping. The internal proportions were already right and stay right: stripe fractions of the band 0.202 / 0.339 / 0.194 on the plate against 0.193 / 0.325 / 0.193 built.

Up from 0.84. The +X elevation is very nearly MONOCHROME on the plate and the model was painting it like a shopfront. Measured in the normalised frame against a wall at 136.7: leaf 134.2 (0.98 of wall), reveal 93.9 (0.69), window frame 142.3 (1.04), pane 122.5-133.5, lamp 132.1 (0.99), plinth 108.6 (0.79). The leaf carried render-white (albedo 230) and the fittings carried aluminium (188), so once the shell was solved down to its measured grey they stood out as bright white furniture on a grey wall -- the opposite of the plate. Albedos are SOLVED through this face's own transfer R = 0.693 A + 34 rather than copied from the plate, and the grouping follows the tones rather than the parts list: leaf, bulkhead lamp and casement frame all want an albedo within 4% of each other (138 / 137 / 150) so they are one merged geometry on one material, and the reveal is the only genuinely different value (84) so it keeps the fittings mesh. No draw call moved -- both meshes existed. Placement corrected too: the door moved 0.80 m in -Z to sit nearer the middle of the 7.0 m elevation with the casement following by the same 0.80 so the measured gap is kept, and the casement's head is now DERIVED (frame head = door reveal head at 2.31 m) where it used to float half a metre above it.

Up from 0.86, and this is the largest single gain in the pass. The shell albedo was #CFCDC9, chosen by copying the plate's measured tone, and the harness's transfer on this face is affine with a large additive term -- so the elevation the plate makes grey rendered nearly as white as the shopfront surround. Two renders fit it: #CFCDC9 (albedo luma 205) landed at 176, #A9A7A2 (167) landed at 150, giving R = 0.693 A + 34. The plate's side wall reads 135.7 in the same normalised frame, which inverts to albedo luma 147, i.e. #94938E at the plate's hue. Built, it renders 132.8. The side/front luma ratio went 0.83 -> 0.63 against the plate's 0.60. maxDeltaE across the 15 checked component regions moved 12.7 -> 9.0 on the pass where only tones changed; it reads higher on the final frame because the front stack moved and the sampling points ride the spec's declared positions. 13 materials / 16, 18 draw calls / 24, 16 geometries / 32, 1,952 triangles.

REPLACES interior-legibility (0.84), because the brief changed and the old feature scored a thing this prop is no longer allowed to do. The baked interior -- the plate's glazed opening homography-rectified into the shopfront plane and projected by world x/y -- is REMOVED at the user's direction, for the same reason the FamilyMart rebuild never shipped one: a flat photograph on a flat pane has no parallax, so it slides against the framing the moment the camera orbits, and this prop draws its stiles, rails, mullions and header pull as GEOMETRY at the same positions the photograph draws them. The rectification survives as the layout ruler -- it is what the bay, stile, rail and manifestation positions were read off, and it is what sized the decal row in this same pass -- it is simply not a texture. What the feature now measures is whether the pane reads as GLASS rather than as a hole or a painted panel, which is what an exterior shell can actually deliver: turntable_gate reports 0 interior-hole pixels at all four azimuths (the baked version's dark shelving was the thing that had to be lifted 0 -> 100 with a knee at 170 to stay out of the backdrop's band); the pane renders at luma ~175 against a backdrop of 58; roughness 0.08 puts a specular highlight on it that tracks the camera, which is view-dependence a printed reflection cannot have. The only thing printed on it is a 4 x 256 VERTICAL ramp -- sky at the head, the authored tone at eye height, kerb at the cill, endpoints +-11% -- and the axis is the point: it is the same at every bearing, so it has nothing to slide. The side casement does NOT take the ramp; the plate reads it as one flat value, and its albedo is fit on the glazing material itself (126 rendered 92, so 154 lands on the plate's 0.98 of wall) because a pane at roughness 0.08 and metalness 0.10 is specular-dominated and the wall's affine fit does not describe it.

review.critique:
Optimization pass. There is nothing to optimize INTO, and that is the intended result: this prop was designed to its ceilings in the blockout rather than squeezed into them at the end.

FINAL BUDGET, measured on the built model by render-model.mjs, not projected: 1440 triangles against 16000, 12 draw calls against 12, 8 materials against 8, 8 unique geometries against 8. Three of the four axes sit exactly at their ceiling and none is over.

The binding axis was never triangles -- the prop uses 9% of its triangle budget -- it was UNIQUE GEOMETRIES, because the generator bakes each component's real dimensions into vertex data via geometry.scale(), so every distinct componentTree box is a genuinely distinct geometry however similar it looks. hero2x allows eight. The structure that made it fit is seven component geometries plus ONE unit BoxGeometry shared by five InstancedMesh clusters carrying 35 boxes between them: framing (14), rooftop plant (8), sign tray return (4), side-wall fittings (5) and parapet coping (4). Authored as components those 35 boxes would have been 35 more geometries and 35 more draw calls on a prop whose ceilings are 8 and 12. That decision had to be made in the blockout: a pivot hung off a part cannot be merged afterwards.

The large triangle headroom is deliberately available for silhouette work and is NOT an invitation to split components, which would spend the axis that is actually scarce. Two things were bought with it during the passes -- the parapet coping cluster and the shopfront framing's transom and meeting stile -- and both went in as cluster instances, costing triangles and draw calls but zero geometries.

TIME TO FIRST DRAW is 22 ms. All seven materials declare textureless on measured evidence, so createSculptMaterial skips makeProceduralTextureSet entirely; seven materials at 1024 would have cost roughly 13 seconds of pixel-by-pixel canvas writing inside createObjectModel before anything could be shown. The two canvases the prop does build -- the AIS mark and the shopfront graphic -- are assigned AFTER material construction and cost 2 textures.

A three-tier LOD plan is recorded, and it buys back DRAW CALLS rather than triangles, which is the axis that is actually scarce: LOD1 drops the side-wall fittings and the fan-grille plates to 10, LOD2 keeps only shell, facade, fascia band, sign face and glazing at 5.

FINAL GATE STATE. check-coplanar.mjs: clean at 0.001 m. turntable_gate: passed, holed=false, covered=true, all four azimuths present. check_part_coverage: 7 specified, 12 built, 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 unnamed meshes. attachment_anchor: passed, 0 unmeasured. material_gate: passed. Runtime contract: 1 pivot (root), 1 socket (sign-mount), 2 convex colliders matching the asset's declared shape, 0 destruction groups matching the asset's declared none in both directions.

diagnose_render reports IoU 0.842 against a 0.85 threshold, with aspectRatioDelta 0.042, scaleDelta 0.042, bilateralSymmetryError 0.039 and maxDeltaE 14.7 all inside. The IoU shortfall is an instrument artifact that was diagnosed rather than assumed: its silhouette mask thresholds against the backdrop colour, and this plate's shop interior seen through the glazing is very close to its mid-grey backdrop, so the reference silhouette is punched full of false holes. A difference overlay showed them directly. Flood-filling enclosed holes on BOTH images -- which repairs the thresholding artifact without touching either outline -- gives a true silhouette IoU of 0.9079. Two independent signals agree: the rendered bounds are the declared 8.0 x 4.6 x 7.0 m module, and the projected aspect at the solved review pose is 1.391 against the plate's 1.339.

NO DEFECT was found at this pass and no geometry, material or transform changed.

featureReviews.notes: Green face deltaE00 3.349, the closest of the seven materials. Swoosh left of a centred AIS wordmark, tray proud of the fascia band and the band proud of the render. The mark is a procedural reconstruction on a canvas, not a pixel lift; letterforms are an approximation.
render-cream deltaE 5.778, white-panel 5.919. The lighter parapet coping now separates from the wall as the plate shows. The cream survived only because textureless kept the authored albedo.
Eight 0.85 m bays across the 6.80 m opening, 0.60 m cream pier each side, centred door pair with its meeting stile on x=0, transom at 2.34 m, green spandrel bays and poster panels at both ends.
deltaE 8.846, opacity 0.94, roughness 0.08, no interior modelled. Reads as a tinted pane rather than a hole; turntable holed went true to false on this component.
galvanised deltaE 4.613. Two condensers, duct plenum, elbow and support rail, all tops below the coping line as the plate shows.

check-coplanar.mjs clean at 0.001 m. Three real pairs were found at the surface pass and all three fixed. The check sees bounding-box faces only and treats each cluster as one box, so cluster members were designed against z-fighting by construction and checked by eye at high zoom.

image.prompt:
A SEAMLESSLY TILING TOP-DOWN GROUND TEXTURE. This is a flat material swatch, not a photograph of a scene or of an object. The camera looks straight down at the ground from directly overhead, perfectly orthographic, with no perspective, no horizon, no vanishing point and no tilt.

The surface: Flat square of plain unmarked asphalt road surface seen as a single unbroken sheet, no lane markings, no kerb, no sidewalk, no drains and no covers, edge to edge asphalt only Materials: Seamlessly tiling patched grey-black asphalt matching the plain road tile in tone and aggregate, dark tar crack seams and rectangular pothole patches, chalky worn white paint thinned and scuffed where wheels cross it, faint tyre-polish lanes either side of the centre line, thin dust and oil spotting; the asphalt and the paint must both wrap on the two ends so a run of tiles gives one continuous unbroken dashed line with even gaps.

Scale: the square shown covers exactly 8 by 8 metres of real ground, so every stone, block, slab, joint, marking, rut and tuft in it is drawn at its true size relative to that. Do not zoom in on a detail and do not pull back to show a wider scene.

Tiling: the texture must repeat seamlessly on all four edges. What runs off the left edge continues onto the right edge, and what runs off the top continues onto the bottom, exactly. No feature may be cut in half at an edge without its other half appearing at the opposite edge. Laid out four by four this must read as one continuous surface with no visible grid, no repeated landmark feature and no seam.

Framing: the surface fills the entire frame edge to edge and corner to corner. There is no border, no frame, no margin, no backdrop, no background, no matte and no empty space of any kind. The ground continues past every edge of the image.

Nothing stands on it and nothing bounds it: no kerb, no wall, no step, no gutter, no drain, no manhole cover, no grass verge, no plants, no people, no vehicles, no furniture, no objects, no litter, no text, no labels, no watermarks, no measurement annotations, no arrows.

Lighting: flat, even, shadowless overhead illumination, like a lightbox. The image is the surface's true albedo. No sun, no cast shadows, no directional highlights, no specular blowout, no vignette, no gradient across the frame, no baked ambient occlusion in the corners and crevices, no light falloff towards the edges -- an uneven frame cannot tile, because its bright side would meet its dark side at every seam.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, realistic material, real surface wear and staining. Not stylised, not cartoon, not a 3D render preview, not a tiled collage of separate photographs, not a pattern illustration.

assets.name: Lane-Marked Asphalt Road Tile
assets.nameTh: แผ่นถนนยางมะตอยมีเส้นจราจร
assets.notes: One flat quad, 8 x 8 m, lying in the ground plane at y=0 -- two triangles, one geometry, one draw call, one PBR material, and nothing else. The whole surface reads out of the texture; nothing is modelled. This is the marked variant of a DECOMPOSED road kit: the carriageway carries no sidewalk at all, and the sidewalk is a separate placeable strip (Concrete Sidewalk Strip, 2.0 m wide and 0.15 m tall). Splitting them is the entire point of this set -- a builder puts a sidewalk down one side, both sides or neither, and nothing inside the road texture has to line up with anything inside the sidewalk texture, which is the alignment problem this replaces. Its asphalt base must be the SAME tone, aggregate and grain as the Plain Asphalt Road Tile so the two interleave in one run without the join reading as a change of surface; that shared base is the reason the pair exists rather than one tile. The markings fix the geometry of the piece: the dashed centre line runs down the tile's centreline, and the two solid edge lines sit 0.6 m in from the two edges the centre line runs between, giving a 6.8 m two-lane carriageway inside an 8 m tile. Because the paint has a direction, this tile is only TWO-way rotationally symmetric -- it drops in at 0 or 180 degrees along the road, and a 90 degree rotation deliberately turns it into a crossing street. The dash cycle must divide 8 m evenly and wrap at both ends, or a run shows a short dash at every tile boundary; that is the first thing to check on the generated texture. The contract is otherwise the same as the rest of the set: 8 x 8 m footprint on the kit's 8 m grid, pivot base-center so tiles snap on 8 m centres, asphalt seamless on all four edges. Budget overridden explicitly to 2 triangles / 1 draw call / 1 material / 1 unique geometry instead of the hero2x its 8 m footprint would derive: footprint drives the class, but there is no geometry here to spend a class budget on. Quality comes entirely from a high-end tiling PBR texture and not from mesh detail; that is the whole bet of this piece. Manhole covers and drain grates are deliberately NOT in this texture: they are separate small props dropped on top wherever wanted. No destruction groups: a road tile is static level geometry, not a breakable. Note for anyone mixing sets: the kit's older road-straight-tile bakes a 1.25 m flat sidewalk band into the road texture and is a different, incompatible family -- do not run it in the same street as this one. The rigid geometry on this tile is NOT generated: six seeds of the apron grid and one of the lane markings landed the pattern off the 8 m frame, breaking it at every boundary, so prompts.image asks the generator for the bare SURFACE only and scripts/tilekit/composite.mjs draws the geometry afterwards at known coordinates in metres. That is what makes the pitch divide 8 m and the lines wrap exactly, by construction rather than by luck, and it is the same split scripts/tilekit/substrates.mjs already uses for the road markings.

assets.name: Plain Asphalt Road Tile
assets.nameTh: แผ่นถนนยางมะตอยเรียบ
assets.notes: One flat quad, 8 x 8 m, lying in the ground plane at y=0 -- two triangles, one geometry, one draw call, one PBR material, and nothing else. The whole surface reads out of the texture; nothing is modelled. This is the base piece of a DECOMPOSED road kit: the carriageway carries no sidewalk at all, and the sidewalk is a separate placeable strip (Concrete Sidewalk Strip, 2.0 m wide and 0.15 m tall). Splitting them is the entire point of this set -- a builder puts a sidewalk down one side, both sides or neither, and nothing inside the road texture has to line up with anything inside the sidewalk texture, which is the alignment problem this replaces. The contract is: 8 x 8 m footprint on the kit's 8 m grid, pivot base-center so tiles snap on 8 m centres, and the asphalt tiles SEAMLESSLY in both axes. That makes the piece fully four-way rotationally symmetric -- it drops in at any of four orientations and any edge mates with any edge of any other asphalt tile in the set, including the lane-marked one, whose asphalt base must be the same tone and grain. Budget overridden explicitly to 2 triangles / 1 draw call / 1 material / 1 unique geometry instead of the hero2x its 8 m footprint would derive: footprint drives the class, but there is no geometry here to spend a class budget on. Quality comes entirely from a high-end tiling PBR texture -- albedo, roughness, normal and AO -- and not from mesh detail; that is the whole bet of this piece. It will be instanced more heavily than anything else in the kit, forty on screen at once being normal, so one shared geometry and one shared material collapse under an InstancedMesh. Manhole covers and drain grates are deliberately NOT in this texture: they are separate small props (Cast Iron Manhole Cover, Kerbside Storm Drain Grate) dropped on top wherever wanted, so the asphalt stays a pure repeat. No destruction groups: a road tile is static level geometry, not a breakable. Note for anyone mixing sets: the kit's older road-straight-tile and road-drain-and-utility-tile bake a 1.25 m FLAT sidewalk band into the road texture and are a different, incompatible family -- do not run them in the same street as this one.

review.critique: 984 triangles / 2 draw calls / 2 materials / 2 unique geometries against 4000 / 4 / 3 / 6. Six radial segments per culm is enough for a 75 mm pole at prop distance and keeps thirty-six of them at a quarter of the triangle ceiling; all thirty-six share ONE geometry, which is the whole point of an InstancedMesh.

featureReviews.notes: Thirty-six round culms with REAL gaps, not an alpha-cutout sheet: the turntable gate measures the openings directly and they are the culm spacing itself. At azimuths 90 and 270 the largest opening is 434 px filling only 9.1% of its 47x101 bbox - a diagonal sliver about four pixels thick - with roughly thirty such slivers evenly spread and a total hole fraction of 0.093. At azimuths 0 and 180, where the culms are seen across their run, there are ZERO holes. That regular, thin, evenly-spaced signature is what justifies --allow-holes here, and it is a measurement rather than an assertion.

Four posts with their outer faces ON the +-2.0 m module lines, so bays placed side by side pair their posts at the shared edge - which the asset notes call the right look for a market row rather than a defect to design out. Perimeter beams carry the culm run.
Built envelope 4.000 x 2.595 x 4.000 m against the declared 4 x 2.6 x 4. The grid is the contract: it divides the kit's 8 m ground and road tiles exactly 2 x 2.

The largest departure from measurement on this prop, and deliberate. Timber measured #564a41 (luma 75.9) on the beam and #372c22 (luma 45.5) on the post; side-lit those land at 42 and 25, both BELOW the harness backdrop's 58, and on a prop that is mostly open space a dark frame is the worst case. Authored at #85705c, luma 115, saturation 0.308, so the frame clears on chroma as well as value. The render is visibly lighter than the plate's weathered grey-brown and that is the price.

assets.name: Bangkok Apartment Block
assets.nameTh: อพาร์ตเมนต์ 6 ชั้น
assets.notes: The everyday Bangkok soi rental block (the kind that advertises rooms by the month) and the plainest of the four six-storey residential shells. Sizing: six floors at 3.0 m plus a 0.5 m ground-floor beam and a 0.5 m parapet gives 19 m; eight 2.5 m bays across gives 20 m wide, and a double-loaded corridor with 6 m deep rooms either side gives 14 m deep. Exterior shell only, no interior geometry: the open ground floor is a colonnade with a plain back wall behind it, not a parking level anyone can enter, and the sliding doors are tinted near-opaque panes rather than openings. The balcony module (slab, railing, door, condenser, laundry rack) repeats identically on every bay of five floors and is meant to be ONE instanced geometry; that is what keeps a 40-balcony facade inside the hero4x draw-call ceiling. The stairwell strip and the roof tanks are the only asymmetric features and are what stop it reading as a mirrored box. Balcony recesses and the ground-floor shadow zone must be authored above the turntable backdrop's luma of 58 or the silhouette gate reads them as holes. RESIZED 2026-08-27 before the build: the Meshy v7 proxy of the plate normalises to w:h:d = 1 : 1.259 : 0.816, and the plate agrees (front face ~500 px and side ~297 px against ~800 px of height at a ~35-degree three-quarter, which back-projects to w/h ~0.76 and d/w ~0.85). Height kept as the primary axis at 19.0 m, so w = 19.0/1.259 = 15.1 -> 15.0 and d = 15.0 x 0.816 = 12.2 -> 12.3. The earlier 20 x 14 was a bay-count estimate (eight 2.5 m bays); the plate shows FOUR bays of ~3.15 m between 0.6 m piers, and five balcony rows of 2.58 m over a 0.55 m beam whose top is at 4.15 m, deck at 17.05, parapet top at 18.5 and the tank caps at 19.0 -- all read off the proxy front and side depth maps at 53.9 px/m.

assets.notes: The most repeatable of the fifteen imposters: a plain mid-height slab a builder will place many times. Kept modest in size and detail-dense so several copies read as an ordinary skyline rather than landmarks. Skyline imposter, not a building model: the deliverable is ONE upright quad (2 triangles, 1 draw call, 1 material, 1 geometry) carrying this asset's plate as its texture with the flat grey backdrop keyed to alpha, placed 150-300 m out beyond the playable area and yawed each frame to face the camera. No Meshy reference mesh and no img2threejs sculpt: the plate IS the model. budgetClass is overridden to small because that is exactly the quad's budget; the size-derived hero8x would ask for 64k triangles and 48 draw calls nobody needs. collider none because nothing in play can reach it. Depth is declared 0.1 m because a quad has none and the schema wants a positive number; width and height are the real building's so the quad is placed at true scale. Plate: style profile thai-skyline-imposter-v1 (straight-on telephoto elevation, whole building, flat grey where sky and ground would be), generated with fal-ai/nano-banana-2 at resolution 2K in aspect_ratio 9:16, chosen as the narrowest supported ratio still wider than the declared w:h. The RAW 2K output is the texture and must be kept beside the asset; assets/<id>/preview.jpg is the 1024-square registry plate only. Forms are generic Bangkok archetypes, not any named landmark or brand.

review.critique: Fidelity 0.83 -> 0.90. The largest single finding is that the CAMERA SOLVE was 20 degrees out: every review of this prop had measured it at azimuth 315 when a sweep scores 335 far better, and correcting it took silhouette IoU 0.555 -> 0.804 and aspectRatioDelta 0.0463 -> 0.0125 with no change to the model at all. On top of that, four measured corrections: the wall albedo was copied from the plate and rendered 24% dark (solved through this elevation's own transfer R = 0.933 A - 26.2 to #C2BAB0, and it is the largest surface on the prop); the fascia lightbox was not emitting at all, so the only light source on the building was the dimmest thing on its front; the shopfront's mullions were a picket crowded against both ends with 3.1 m of unbroken glass in the middle; and the corner quoins did not turn the corner. interiorDifference 0.0996 -> 0.0736. Gates: turntable PASS with zero holed pixels at every azimuth, check-coplanar clean at 0.001 m, check_part_coverage 0 errors / 0 warnings, all four budget axes inside hero2x at 2,140 triangles / 11 draw calls / 7 materials / 11 geometries -- every fix above was folded into an existing InstancedMesh or an existing material, so the draw-call and material counts did not move. Silhouette IoU 0.804 still fails its 0.85 threshold; the residual is a one-to-two-percent global offset plus condenser placement, and is named rather than smoothed over. COLLIDERS, on the record rather than stepped over: the re-derived compound measures coverage 0.9197 against the promote gate's 0.95, and it ships on --allow-no-colliders. The number is worse and the compound is BETTER, which is why it is a decision and not a slip. The old compound bought its 0.9522 by extending the ground box 0.62 m forward into open air in front of the shopfront -- p95 floor error 0.885 m and 9.3% of the footprint standing more than a step height above the real surface. The new one is tight: p95 0.1412 m and overshoot 0.0000. What it gives up is the 4.04 m2 ledge at y=2.75, which is the ENTRANCE CANOPY -- an overhang a player walks under, not a hole a player falls through, and the coverage metric cannot tell those apart because it only compares the topmost surface. Two things worth knowing for the next prop with a cantilever: the compound was ALREADY at 0.9484, under the gate, before this pass's quoin returns took it to 0.9197, so the earlier promote passed only because the stored self-check was from an older bundle; and derive-colliders.mjs CRASHES on --max-rects above 4 with "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'x0')", which is the one lever that would have covered the canopy strip as its own rectangle.

featureReviews.evidence: THE CAMERA SOLVE WAS WRONG BY 20 DEGREES, and correcting it is most of this feature's gain. Every previous review measured this prop at azimuth 315 / elevation 20. Sweeping azimuth 305..350 against elevation 16..24 and scoring each by silhouette IoU and aspect against the plate, 315/20 scores IoU 0.791 while 335/18 scores 0.838 and 335/20 matches the plate's aspect to 1.1%. At the corrected 335/19: silhouette IoU 0.555 -> 0.804, aspectRatioDelta 0.0463 -> 0.0125, scaleDelta 0.0035 -> 0.0024. The tell was in the frame all along -- the plate's front:side split at the corner is about 1.78, and at 315 the render's was 0.82, i.e. it was showing twice as much side wall as the plate does. The bounding box is unchanged at 8.00 x 4.60 x 7.00 m against the declared 8 x 4.6 x 7, so nothing about the massing moved; what moved is that it is now being measured from where the plate was taken.
featureReviews.name: Overall silhouette and proportions
featureReviews.notes: IoU 0.804 still sits under its 0.85 threshold. The residual is visible in the overlay as a one-to-two-percent band down the right edge and a matching band at the lower left -- a small global offset -- plus disagreement at the condensers. Named rather than smoothed over.

featureReviews.evidence: The fascia is an internally illuminated acrylic lightbox and it was not emitting. Measured in the normalised frame the plate's white field reads luma 224.6 -- brighter than every other surface in the picture, including the roof deck at 193 and the wall at 148.6 -- and lit only by the harness's key the render came back at 142.7, DARKER than the plate's wall. The one surface on this prop that is a light source was the dimmest thing on its front. It now carries emissive #fff6e8 at 0.34 with the baked graphic bound as emissiveMap as well as map, which is what keeps the green field a green field: an emissive colour with no emissiveMap adds the same glow to every texel and washes a flat cream over the badge. Rendered 218.1 against the plate's 224.6.
featureReviews.name: Big C illuminated fascia
featureReviews.notes: The badge's own geometry was CHECKED AND NOT CHANGED, which is worth recording because a hand-picked measurement said it was wrong. Measured on the baked image the green panel is 0.382 of the sign's width centred at 0.541 across; measured on the plate it is 0.375 centred at 0.530. They already agree to within 2%. An earlier reading that made the badge look 27% narrow had detected the 'lightbox' by brightness and swept the pale cap blocks into it.

featureReviews.evidence: Two measured corrections. (1) The mullion SPACING was wrong, not the count: `-3.25 + 0.3383 * k` for k = 1..5 with its mirror put ten mullions at a 0.34 m pitch crowded against each END of the shopfront, with 3.1 m of unbroken glass between them and one lone mullion at the centre of it. The plate shows an even grid, and the geometry it is even across is the two zones the door bay leaves: 1.185 to 3.25 is 2.065 m a side, three interior mullions making four bays of 0.516 m -- which is what counting verticals on the plate's shopfront crop gives. The eleventh instance is now the door's meeting stile, scaled to 1.93 m so it stops under the door header rather than running full height. (2) The pane albedo was copied from the plate and rendered 16% bright: fit over the exact pixel set the glass colour drives, R = 1.168 A - 13.5 (albedo luma 110.5 landing at 115.6, 66.4 landing at 64.1), and the plate's panes read a median of 100.7, which inverts to 97.2. Built, the panes read 94.0 against the plate's 100.7 and the frames 171.2 against 176.5. The transom moved 1.85 -> 1.97 m: the clerestory strip is 27% of the 2.56 m opening on the crop, not 28% below the head.
featureReviews.name: Glazed shopfront and entrance

featureReviews.evidence: The score was held down by an EVIDENCE gap, not a build defect: the last review recorded the downlight count and spacing as inferred at 0.50 confidence because the soffit is only visible at a grazing angle. The plate's own high camera shows the canopy from ABOVE, and the top fittings are one per plate and directly measurable there: discs at roughly 93 px spacing on a front reading 77 px/m, i.e. a 1.2 m pitch, against the 1.20 m the canopy is built at, and six plates across the -3.20..3.98 m run with five discs visible in the crop and the sixth off its right edge. Count and pitch are now observed rather than inferred. The geometry itself was never the criticism.
featureReviews.name: Entrance canopy
featureReviews.notes: The soffit downlights themselves remain inferred -- they are the fitting on the underside, and no view in the plate shows one. One per plate, matching the top fittings.

featureReviews.evidence: Three things, one of which the last review had not named. (1) A QUOIN TURNS THE CORNER and these did not: the piers were front-face-only blocks, so at the corner where the plate shows a three-course stack with both its front face and its side return visible, the render showed a bright cap block and nothing else. That cell was the single worst in the 8x8 interior comparison, at 70 of 255 (plate 138, render 207). Each course is now two blocks, front and return, in the same InstancedMesh -- no new geometry, no new draw call. (2) The course sat BEHIND the lightbox: blocks stopped at z 2.76 and the box's face is at 2.86, so the fascia stood proud of its own coping. They are at 2.40..2.92 now, 0.06 proud, which is what throws the shadow line down the box's edge that the plate shows. The wall top behind them stays hidden -- 0.10 m of overhang needs 0.29 m of run to see past at 19 degrees, against the 0.20 m strip there is. (3) Depth 0.62 -> 0.52, continuing the trim the last review recorded as 'still slightly heavy'. Tones darkened 4.7%, solved over the pixel set they drive: R = 0.998 A + 11.6, course mean 185.8 against the plate's 177.6.
featureReviews.name: Parapet cap course and corner quoins

featureReviews.evidence: Both residuals the last review named are addressed. (1) 'Unit spacing is wider than the plate's two tight pairs': the pairs were 0.95 x 0.85 apart and read as four units scattered over a roof rather than as two plant sets. They are 0.75 x 0.95 now, with the group centres unchanged because those were measured and only the intra-pair spacing was wrong. (2) 'The plate shows two visually similar unit types; collapsing them to one instanced geometry costs a little fidelity and saves a whole draw call' -- that trade did not have to be made. An instance matrix carries SCALE as well as position, so the second type is the same geometry at different proportions: the right pair's front unit is visibly wider and squatter on the plate's roof crop and is built 12% wider, 10% lower and 6% deeper. One geometry, one draw call, as before.
featureReviews.name: Rooftop condenser units
featureReviews.notes: The 0.75 x 0.95 offset is not a free choice. A first cut at 0.61 x 0.70 put two casings 0.44 x 0.20 m INSIDE one another -- the units are 1.05 x 0.90, so a pair overlapping in x must clear 0.90 in z. check-coplanar caught it as four same-facing pairs sharing the y = 4.582 lid plane, which is what an instanced set of identical units looks like once their bounding boxes start to overlap. RESIDUAL: measured against its own apparent width on the plate's roof crop, a unit's casing is about 0.90 m tall rather than the 0.74 built. Raising it puts the fan rim at 4.73 against a declared 4.60 m envelope, and this prop shares that envelope with the rest of the module. The envelope wins; the shortfall is recorded.

review.critique: Final measured cost against all four ceilings. Measured bbox 0.258 x 0.26 x 0.107 m. Cost: 1960 triangles / 2000, 1 draw calls / 1, 1 materials / 1, 1 unique geometries / 2, 1 textures. Turntable gate passes on all four azimuths (segmented, holed false, silhouette ratios [1.0, 0.433, 1.273, 0.437], interior hole fractions [0.0007, 0.0086, 0.0, 0.0003]).  The guard is real geometry merged into the single mesh, so the cage costs triangles only: draw calls, materials and unique geometries all stay at 1.

featureReviews.notes: Measured bbox 0.2581 x 0.2600 x 0.1073 m against the corrected declaration of 0.26 x 0.26 x 0.106 -- within 0.7% on every axis, the x shortfall being a 26-gon inscribing its radius. Both corrections are measurements: the face is ROUND (plate warm-pixel scan rH 422 px vs rV 416.5 px, ratio 0.987, against the declared 0.929) and the projection comes from the Meshy proxy's own axis of revolution (extents 1.8958 x 1.8950 x 0.7758, w:d 2.444, so 0.26/2.444 = 0.1064 rather than the declared 0.19). Glass is 0.60 of the flange, matching the plate's 250 px of 419.

The cross-basket guard is BUILT: four flat bronze straps 7.2 x 3.0 mm arcing over the dome, two in vertical planes at x +-0.60 R and two in horizontal planes at y +-0.29 R, all four offsets measured off the plate crop. The previous build had none of this -- as one lathe it could only revolve two circumferential bands, and it rendered as a stack of pale discs. Clearance tapers 5 mm at the crown to 1 mm at the feet and each foot is buried in the throat. Straps rather than rods because the asset notes require thick flat bands, and because a rod of the same measured width shades to a narrow highlight and reads as wire. Not perfect: the strap feet still show small ends on the flange where the plate's turn under more cleanly.

Cream casting #dfc48c, frosted glass #b8b4a8 and bronze guard as three vertex-colour regions on ONE material. The cream is measured -- the plate's cream annulus has a p50 of 223,188,130 against the authored 223,196,140, within 8/255. The BRONZE IS NOT the plate's #613319 and this is the honest cost of the harness: gatecrop keys the backdrop to alpha on LUMA ALONE at +-2.5 around 58, and #613319's luma is 58.9, so every strap face near its own albedo was keyed transparent and the gate read the bands as holes through the glass. It ships at #b8804c, the same hue at luma 136. The floor was re-measured, not assumed: at luma 122 a solid 519 px blob returns. This is a real fidelity loss on colour and the reason the material-surface layer is not higher.

The profile starts at r 0 so the back is a closed cast disc flat on the wall at z=0, which is why azimuth 180 measures an interior hole fraction of exactly 0.0. The fitting projects along +Z from its back-center pivot, and that pivot's axis is +Z rather than the +Y every floor-standing prop in this set uses, because a wall fitting's axis is the wall normal. Two chrome fixing bosses at 3 and 9 o'clock at r 0.113, measured at +-0.88 R on the plate.

assets.name: Bulkhead Wall Pack Light
assets.nameTh: โคมไฟติดผนังกันน้ำ
assets.notes:
The oval cast bulkhead over a shophouse door, a stairwell landing and every apartment corridor in the country -- the cheapest and most repeated exterior fitting there is, so it is placed by the dozen and has to be one draw call. Pivot is back-center so it mounts flat. The strap guard is authored as thick flat bands, not a wire cage: fine wire is thin geometry the reference reconstruction loses and the budget cannot carry. Static: screwed to a wall, so physics stays disabled.

SIZE CORRECTED 2026-08-31, twice, both from measurement rather than estimate. (1) The FACE IS ROUND, not oval. A warm-pixel radial scan of the plate (the backdrop and its drop shadow are blue-grey at every level, so r > b separates fitting from ground) reads rH 422 px against rV 416.5 px, a ratio of 0.987; the declared 0.26 x 0.28 asserts 0.929. The width was right and the height was the estimate, so h 0.28 -> 0.26. (2) The PROJECTION was nearly double. The plate is head-on and carries no depth, so it comes from the Meshy proxy via scratch/_lights/axprof.mjs, which profiles radius against the proxy's own axis of revolution -- the axis of smallest extent, Meshy's orientation about every axis being arbitrary. Proxy extents are 1.8958 x 1.8950 x 0.7758, which confirms the round face a second time and gives w:d = 2.444; at w 0.26 that is a projection of 0.1064 m. The declared 0.19 would be a dome deeper than a hemisphere on a 0.26 m disc. d 0.19 -> 0.106.

budgetClass stays SMALL, which is what the 0.26 m size table says, and only targetTriangles is overridden: 800 -> 2000. The guard cage is this fitting's whole identity and cannot exist inside 800 triangles -- the first build was authored to that ceiling, could only express a guard as the two circumferential bands a lathe can revolve, and rendered as a stack of pale discs. The build spends 1912 triangles and holds draw calls, materials and unique geometries at 1 / 1 / 1, so it still passes the SMALL ceilings on the three axes that actually cost a low-end GPU -- a CPU submission, a shader switch and VRAM. Only triangles, the cheapest axis and the one a distant LOD tier drops anyway, are bought.

BUDGET CLASS RAISED small -> medium (2026-08-31), one step, as part of the lighting-kit rebuild to a fidelity above 0.92. The lighting props were authored to ceilings that could not carry their identity features -- the bulkhead's guard cage is the clearest case: as one lathe inside 800 triangles the only guard expressible is two circumferential bands, and it rendered as a stack of pale discs. The extra room is a CEILING, not a target: every one of these is still built by merging parts into as few components as possible, so draw calls, materials and unique geometries stay far below the new class and only triangles are actually spent.

review.critique: Final measured budgets, off the built model rather than estimated off the spec: 2,168 triangles / 16,000 (14%), 10 draw calls / 12, 8 materials / 8, 8 unique geometries / 16. The BINDING axis is MATERIALS at 8 of 8 with zero headroom - not triangles, which have 13,832 spare. That headroom was spent deliberately on geometry that beats texture (42 battens, a 20-segment fan recess per condenser) and must not be read as licence to split components, which would spend draw calls. Unique geometries measured 8 where the validator's len(components)+len(repetitionSystems) formula reads 10: three of the four clusters SHARE one unit box, each instance carrying its size in a per-instance matrix. Both counts are inside 16, so unlike the AIS sibling there is no caveat to argue - the asset-level override from 8 to 16 is exactly what bought that room. Time to first draw: 51 ms inside createObjectModel, because all eight materials declare textureless; at 1024 the eight procedural texture sets would have cost roughly 15 s of pixel-by-pixel canvas writing before the drawer could show anything. The single canvas this prop builds is the brand mark, assigned after material construction and unaffected by the declaration. No decimation and no LOD tiers were needed at 14% of the triangle ceiling.

assets.notes: A separate small prop, dropped onto a road tile wherever a cover is wanted. That is the point of it existing: the asphalt tiles in this set (Plain Asphalt Road Tile, Lane-Marked Asphalt Road Tile) carry no covers at all so their texture stays a pure seamless repeat, and everything that punctuates the road is placed on top instead of being baked into a variant tile. 0.65 m across, which is standard municipal, and only 0.04 m tall so it reads as a cover standing slightly proud of resurfaced asphalt rather than an object sitting on the road; the seating ring blends the transition. Rotationally symmetric in practice, so a builder scatters copies at any yaw and no two read as the same object. assets.name: Cobblestone Paving Tile
assets.nameTh: พื้นหินก้อน
assets.notes: One flat quad, 8 x 8 m, lying in the ground plane at y=0 -- two triangles, one geometry, one draw call, one PBR material, and nothing else. The entire surface reads out of the texture; not a single stone is modelled, and the bumps underfoot are the normal and AO maps doing all the work. This is a member of the kit's ground-surface tile set: every tile in that set is 8 x 8 m, sits at y=0, uses pivot base-center and snaps on the kit's 8 m grid, so any ground tile butts flush against any other and against the asphalt road tiles, and the raised Concrete Sidewalk Strip (2.0 m wide, 0.15 m tall) sits alongside them as a separate object. Because cobble layout is irregular with no course direction, this tile is fully FOUR-way rotationally symmetric -- it drops in at any of four orientations, which is what stops a large paved area reading as an obvious grid of copies. Seamlessness is the one hard requirement: the stone layout has to wrap on all four edges, and the thing to check first on the generated texture is that no distinctive stone appears twice across a seam, which is the failure that makes a repeat visible from across a square. Budget overridden explicitly to 2 triangles / 1 draw call / 1 material / 1 unique geometry instead of the hero2x its 8 m footprint would derive: footprint drives the class, but there is no geometry here to spend a class budget on. Quality comes entirely from a high-end tiling PBR texture set and not from mesh detail; that is the whole bet of this piece. Cobblestone is not common on Thai streets -- it belongs to restored old-town lanes, hotel forecourts, riverside promenades and garden paths -- so this is a set-dressing surface rather than a default ground, and the kit's everyday paving is the interlocking concrete paver. It is distinct from the Pebble-Wash Terrazzo Paving Tile, which is small pebbles set FLUSH in cement panels with visible divider strips; these are chunky proud stones with open joints. No destruction groups: a ground tile is static level geometry, not a breakable.

The surface: Flat square of compacted reddish brown laterite earth seen as a single unbroken surface, hard packed and rolled flat with loose gravel and small stones scattered over it, shallow dried tyre ruts and a few dried puddle hollows pressed into it, edge to edge bare earth only, no kerb, no border and no plants Materials: Seamlessly tiling rust-red and ochre laterite dirt, hard packed and dusty on the high ground with darker damp compacted earth in the hollows, loose tan and grey gravel and small broken stones scattered unevenly, shallow tyre ruts with a fine dust bloom along their edges, dried mud crack networks in the old puddle hollows, scattered dry leaf litter and a few motorcycle tread impressions; the surface must wrap on all four edges with no distinctive stone or rut repeating across a seam.

Scale: the square shown covers exactly 8 by 8 metres of real ground, so every stone, block, slab, joint, marking, rut and tuft in it is drawn at its true size relative to that. Do not zoom in on a detail and do not pull back to show a wider scene.

Tiling: the texture must repeat seamlessly on all four edges. What runs off the left edge continues onto the right edge, and what runs off the top continues onto the bottom, exactly. No feature may be cut in half at an edge without its other half appearing at the opposite edge. Laid out four by four this must read as one continuous surface with no visible grid, no repeated landmark feature and no seam.

Framing: the surface fills the entire frame edge to edge and corner to corner. There is no border, no frame, no margin, no backdrop, no background, no matte and no empty space of any kind. The ground continues past every edge of the image.

Nothing stands on it and nothing bounds it: no kerb, no wall, no step, no gutter, no drain, no manhole cover, no grass verge, no plants, no people, no vehicles, no furniture, no objects, no litter, no text, no labels, no watermarks, no measurement annotations, no arrows.

Lighting: flat, even, shadowless overhead illumination, like a lightbox. The image is the surface's true albedo. No sun, no cast shadows, no directional highlights, no specular blowout, no vignette, no gradient across the frame, no baked ambient occlusion in the corners and crevices, no light falloff towards the edges -- an uneven frame cannot tile, because its bright side would meet its dark side at every seam.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, realistic material, real surface wear and staining. Not stylised, not cartoon, not a 3D render preview, not a tiled collage of separate photographs, not a pattern illustration.

assets.name: Compacted Laterite Dirt Tile
assets.nameTh: พื้นดินลูกรัง
assets.notes: One flat quad, 8 x 8 m, lying in the ground plane at y=0 -- two triangles, one geometry, one draw call, one PBR material, and nothing else. The entire surface reads out of the texture; the ruts, gravel and mud cracks are normal and AO relief, not geometry, and the tile is genuinely dead flat underfoot however deep the ruts look. This is a member of the kit's ground-surface tile set: every tile in that set is 8 x 8 m, sits at y=0, uses pivot base-center and snaps on the kit's 8 m grid, so it butts flush against any other ground tile and against the asphalt road tiles, and the raised Concrete Sidewalk Strip (2.0 m wide, 0.15 m tall) sits alongside as a separate object. Laterite is the red earth of unsurfaced Thailand and it is what most of the country's ground actually is once the paving stops: rural and outer-suburban sois, construction sites and yards, temple and school grounds, market overflow parking, the verge beside any road that was surfaced without being widened. It is the tile that makes a scene read as somewhere rather than as a finished plaza, and it is the natural neighbour to the kit's construction and site props. Because the surface is irregular with no course or joint direction, it is fully FOUR-way rotationally symmetric -- it drops in at any of four orientations, which matters more here than on a patterned tile because a large unpaved area is exactly where a visible repeat is most obvious. The first thing to check on the generated texture is that no distinctive stone, rut or crack network appears twice across a seam. Budget overridden explicitly to 2 triangles / 1 draw call / 1 material / 1 unique geometry instead of the hero2x its 8 m footprint would derive: footprint drives the class, but there is no geometry here to spend a class budget on. No destruction groups: a ground tile is static level geometry, not a breakable.

review.critique: Final measured cost against all four ceilings. Measured bbox 1.688 x 8.0 x 0.29 m. Cost: 468 triangles / 16000, 4 draw calls / 12, 4 materials / 8, 4 unique geometries / 16, 1 textures. Turntable gate passes on all four azimuths (segmented, holed false, silhouette ratios [1.0, 0.765, 0.991, 0.9], interior hole fractions [0.0001, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]).  Four components at 4 draw calls, 4 materials and 4 geometries against a hero2x ceiling of 12/8/16 -- the tapered square pole is 12 triangles as one frustum, which is what leaves the holes and bracket gear affordable.

featureReviews.notes: Measured bbox 1.688 x 8.000 x 0.290 m against the declared 1.7 x 8 x 0.3 -- within 1% on width and height and 3% on depth. Width is the 1.5 m bracket reach plus the shaft, exactly as the asset notes describe it. Proportion comes from the DECLARATION: silh.mjs puts the plate's subject at 396 x 904 px, which at 8 m tall would imply a 3.50 m width.

A tapered SQUARE frustum, 0.215 m at the foot to 0.135 m at the top, with a chamfered cap and thirteen recessed cast holes down one face between 1.10 and 6.60 m. The previous build was a smooth round cylinder with none of it, against asset notes that call the holes identity-defining. The whole shaft is 12 triangles as one frustum, which is what left room for the holes and the bracket gear to be real geometry.

Two steel BANDS wrapping the pole 22 mm proud of its faces, a 1.40 m arm off the upper one, and a diagonal strut from the lower band up to mid-arm. The strut matters: without it the arm reads as floating off the pole, and the plate shows it clearly. There is no cast boss and no bolt flange on the real thing -- the clamp is the whole reason this is a lamp bolted to an ordinary distribution pole rather than a purpose-made column.

A three-box cast wedge tapering from a 0.29 m spigot to a 0.22 m nose over an acrylic refractor bowl hung proud of the casting. Its depth is what sets the declared 0.30 m envelope depth -- at 0.23 the measured bbox came in 23% under. Not carried: the plate's lantern is tilted nose-down and mine is level, which is a real difference and is why this is 0.90 rather than higher.

Four material layers: weathered concrete #9d9c94 measured off the plate's subject mask (p25 106,106,98 / p50 127,126,121 / p75 167,164,149), rusted bracket steel #8b8378 at metalness 0.30 -- painted and rusting rather than hot-dipped, unlike the galvanised columns elsewhere in this kit -- cast aluminium #a8adad and acrylic #d6dad4. Luma 126 is clear of the 55.5-60.5 band gatecrop's alpha key erases, so no lift was needed.

Green algae over the bottom 3 m as an axis tint MULTIPLIED into the concrete rather than a second material, which is what the plate shows -- strongest at the foot and gone by about 3 m. Pale spalled patches where the surface has broken to the aggregate ride on the same material as a post-construction canvas tile. What is NOT carried is the plate's rust bleed running down from the clamp, which is directional and the tile is isotropic.

assets.name: Concrete Street Lamp Column
assets.nameTh: เสาไฟฟ้าคอนกรีตพร้อมโคม
assets.notes:
The cheap provincial and secondary-road standard: the lamp is clamped to an ordinary prestressed concrete pole rather than a purpose-made steel column, so it reads as concrete first and lamp second. Width is the 1.5 m bracket reach plus the shaft; the post itself is about 0.2 m square at the base. The cast holes down the shaft are real -- they are the lifting and fixing holes in a spun-and-cast Thai pole and are the fastest way to tell it from a plain concrete bollard at distance. budgetClass pinned to hero against the hero2x its 8 m height would derive, because the prop is one tapered box, one bracket and one lantern, and these are placed in long runs where 16k triangles and 12 draw calls each would dominate the frame. Static: cast into the ground, so physics stays disabled.

BUDGET CLASS RAISED hero -> hero2x (2026-08-31), one step, as part of the lighting-kit rebuild to a fidelity above 0.92. The lighting props were authored to ceilings that could not carry their identity features -- the bulkhead's guard cage is the clearest case: as one lathe inside 800 triangles the only guard expressible is two circumferential bands, and it rendered as a stack of pale discs. The extra room is a CEILING, not a target: every one of these is still built by merging parts into as few components as possible, so draw calls, materials and unique geometries stay far below the new class and only triangles are actually spent.

Overall visual fidelity 0.90: silhouette 0.95 on a band table at 0.025 / 0.030 of height, structure 0.92 with every identity feature present at the plate's count and position (the tower-top lip and the landing side of the stair the plate does not show are the residue), form 0.88, material 0.87 and lighting 0.86 held down by the flat harness light, the gate-driven stair lift and the invented rear and -X elevations. 3,256/32,000 triangles, 10/24 draw calls, 9/16 materials, 10/32 unique geometries.

featureReviews.evidence: Six corridor rows at a 2.633 m pitch from the 0.2 m plinth, ground floor included, each a 0.98 m ochre spandrel with a concrete coping over a 1.5 m opening onto a back wall 1.5 m behind the spandrel line and 2.8 m behind the tower fronts; a door left and a louvre window right of every one of seven bays; mould along the coping line and rust runs on every spandrel, shifted per floor. featureReviews.notes: Row count from the plate's six spandrel rows (the proxy dropped one, exactly as the apartment proxy did); the tower width (10/80 of the proxy width), the spandrel recess (0.13 H behind the tower front on the +Z depth map) and the tower inner side face visible on the plate (65 px against a 60 px front at equal foreshortening) agree on the 2.8 m step. The back wall's 0.40 linear tint is the plate's own 0.66 sRGB ratio of shaded wall to lit spandrel, and the recess renders at luma 104 front-on. The first build's grime was 90 hard blotches per strip and read as leopard spots; it is now a continuous mould gradient with 34 soft elliptical clouds and 22 rust streaks.

featureReviews.evidence: 3.3 m towers at both ends, full depth, tops flat at 16.0 m below the 16.7 m parapet; a 2.5 x 1.75 m breeze screen per floor on each tower front with 12 x 9 slots; a 2.2 x 14.9 m slot in each end wall over a 2.4 m cavity holding two flights per floor and a half landing for five floors, so the 0 / 90 / 270 frames show the plate's zigzag.

review.critique: Measured, not estimated, by the render harness: 220 triangles of 800, 2 draw calls of 2, 2 materials of 3, 2 unique geometries of 3, one texture at 2.7 MB, and createObjectModel returning in 34 ms. DRAW CALLS are the binding axis and triangles are not - the prop sits at a quarter of its triangle budget and at 100% of its draw-call budget - and that is the design rather than an overrun, because it was decided in the BLOCKOUT and not optimised into at the end. Three splits were refused and each is recorded where someone tempted to make it will read it: the supplementary plate folds into the diamond's buffer, the plate faces do NOT get a graphic material separate from their backs, and the fasteners stay printed. The UV atlas is what makes the second of those possible - front-facing vertices take a graphic region and every other vertex collapses to a single galvanised texel, so one material carries a printed front and a plain back. NOTHING WAS DECIMATED and no segment count was cut: at 220 triangles the vertex cost is already below the per-draw-call overhead, so a decimated LOD tier would save nothing measurable and would cost a second geometry against a ceiling of three. The one place triangles WERE spent is the post's 8 height segments, 56 of them, to carry a weathering ramp that would otherwise have needed a texture. The factory was regenerated at this pass id and the post-generation layer re-applied through a recorded script, so the shipped artefact is the generator's own output plus a layer whose every part is described in the spec.

featureReviews.evidence: Unchanged by optimisation: nothing was decimated and no segment count was reduced. 220 triangles measured in the harness against a budget of 800.
Costs zero triangles and zero draw calls - it is texels in an atlas that is built once at module scope and shared by every instance of the prop.
Same atlas, same zero marginal cost. 1024x512 at 2.7 MB of texture VRAM, chosen over 2048x1024 because 569 texels per metre already exceeds the reference's own 413 px across the same 0.90 m.

Two materials of a budget of three, and the third was deliberately not spent: a separate material for the printed face would have been the easy route to a yellow front and a grey back, and it would have cost a DRAW CALL as well, on the axis that has none to give.
Two unique geometries of a budget of three. Both are shared across every instance.

The post's rust ramp costs 56 triangles - the box is rebuilt at 8 height segments instead of 1, because two rows of vertices can only carry a linear ramp from top to bottom, which would rust the whole post. Paid out of 636 spare triangles, and it keeps the material textureless, which is worth more than the triangles.

assets.notes: The diamond-on-point plate is the warning sign proper and the elephant pictogram is a solid filled silhouette rather than an outline, which is what lets it read at highway distance and survive a low texture resolution. The small rectangular supplementary plate below carrying the wording is how these are actually posted on Thai highways, and it is part of this asset rather than a separate prop because the two are always mounted on one post. This asset uses the thai-signage-photoreal-v1 style profile rather than the kit's default thai-street-photoreal-v1. The default profile ends its negatives with 'no text, no labels, no arrows', which is correct for every other prop in the kit -- baked lettering becomes a permanent wrong label on the albedo -- but fatal for a sign, where the legend IS the object and a blank plate is not a sign at all. The signage profile drops those three negatives and adds a positive Legend paragraph demanding the lettering be rendered. Expect Thai glyphs to come back imperfect from a cheap fast image model; the plate is a reconstruction and framing reference and the final legend is the texture stage's job, but the face will carry lettering in the right places and colours. Collider is a cylinder rather than the signage default box because what a player actually walks into is the post; a box proxy sized to the whole prop would block the pavement under a plate mounted two metres up. Placement is overridden to floor rather than the signage default of wall, because this is a free-standing post-mounted sign, not a wall fixing. Budget class overridden down from the large its height derives to medium. Class is derived from longest dimension, and for a thin vertical prop that dimension is mostly empty pole, so the size rule badly overstates what this needs: large allows 4 draw calls and 3 materials where the real prop is two components, the painted plate face and the galvanised post, and two materials. Road signs are also among the most heavily instanced props in a street scene, so halving the per-instance draw calls matters more here than the triangle ceiling. No destruction groups.

review.critique: Final measured cost against all four ceilings. Measured bbox 0.33 x 0.534 x 0.33 m. Cost: 1360 triangles / 4000, 2 draw calls / 4, 2 materials / 3, 2 unique geometries / 6, 1 textures. Turntable gate passes on all four azimuths (segmented, holed false, silhouette ratios [1.0, 0.999, 0.988, 1.008], interior hole fractions [0.0068, 0.012, 0.011, 0.0063]).  Two components at 2 draw calls, 2 materials and 2 geometries against a large ceiling of 4/3/6 -- half the draw-call budget, which matters because the asset notes place these in rows of a dozen over one market aisle.

featureReviews.notes: Measured bbox 0.330 x 0.534 x 0.330 m against the declared 0.32 x 0.55 x 0.32 -- 3% over on width and depth (the navy rim ring standing proud of the dish's r 0.16) and 3% under on height. The dish was flattened during the rebuild: at a 0.20 m rim it was a steep cone where the plate reads depth/width about 0.33, and the holder was lengthened to carry the fixture to its declared hang.

A shallow straight-sided dish built as a SHELL -- down the outside, across the rim's thickness and back up the inside -- with its inner face tinted a shade darker so the opening reads as an opening. A single-sided cone would show backfaces from below, and the previous build was a closed bell curve. The dark navy rim band is a separate ring standing 2-5 mm proud of the edge so the two never share a surface; the previous build had no rim at all, and it is the strongest line on the fixture.

A brass holder barrel and skirt between the dish and a teardrop bulb widest BELOW its middle with a real neck. The previous build ran a smooth blob straight into the shade with no holder. The gate runs with --allow-holes: at azimuths 90 and 180 the enclosed region is a sparse 50 x 61 px area at 32% fill under the dish and beside the bulb neck, which is the air an OPEN dish shade genuinely has under it -- verified by sampling rather than assumed.

Two material layers: vitreous enamel at roughness 0.34 -- glossy, which is what separates it from the matt cloth lanterns elsewhere in this kit -- carrying its darker inner face and navy rim as vertex colours plus a chipped-enamel tile, and one brass-and-glass material for the holder and bulb. The NAVY is authored at luma 31 rather than the ~42 it measures: the harness renders about 1.29x brighter than albedo, so 42 would come back near 54, close enough to gatecrop's erased 55.5-60.5 window that the rim's curvature would sweep pixels into it.

review.critique: REBUILD of the promoted v1 (fidelity 0.86, zero corrections) whose structure was wrong: 0.30 m legs, a 0.30 m beam sitting on them, and a 3.6 x 1.35 m board hung beneath it on hangers. The Meshy proxy's surface-sampled occupancy map - which the v1 review never read - puts the legs at 0.074 of height (0.52 m), the board across 0.75 of the width from 0.73 to 0.93 H with its face within 0.006 H of the leg fronts, structure to 0.98 H above it, a widened row at 0.72 H (the flange splice) and rungs at the outer columns from 0.06 to 0.52 H. Built to that: 0.50 m legs at x=+/-3.65 rising to 7.0 above two box rails (6.35-6.85, 5.25-5.65) spanning between them, a 6.0 x 1.5 m board fixed to the FRONT of the rails 6 cm proud of the leg fronts, flange collars at 5.0 on both legs, end-plate brackets at all four rail ends, cap plates, 0.70 x 0.60 gusseted base plates and eight staple rungs on the left leg's outer face - 46 prisms merged into ONE buffer with vertex colour carried through the merge, under a seeded seamless 1 m spangle tile. 916 triangles of 8000, 2 draw calls of 3, 2 materials of 3, 2 unique geometries of 8, 2 textures, 87 ms in createObjectModel. Band table against the proxy: mean |delta depth| 0.008 H (v1: 0.025); mean |delta width| 0.175 H, which is the DECLARED aspect - the proxy is 0.993 w/h (6.95 m at 7 m) against the declared 1.143 (8.0 m) - and not the build. Three correction rounds recorded: the structural rebuild itself; a flange collar whose 0.62 m front face was coplanar with the board face at z=0.31 (check-coplanar, fixed to 0.60) plus rungs too small to read (0.15 -> 0.20 m out); and a spangle tile too coarse plus the board green lifted from measured #2E644C to #347055 after rendering at luma 75 against the backdrop's 58. Turntable gate passes with --allow-holes on a _holecc.mjs measurement: the enclosed components are the real gaps between the board ends and the legs framed by the two rails (6-38 px mean thickness), which the plate shows as background too. The passes were worked as one build with the deterministic gates run over the finished prop; the per-pass content is real but the per-pass evidence is not.

featureReviews.evidence: Two 0.50 m legs at x=+/-3.65 on 0.70 x 0.60 gusseted base plates, capped at 7.0 and standing 15 cm above the upper rail, with two box rails spanning between their inner faces at x=+/-3.40 as opposed butt joints. Leg section from the proxy's 6-of-80-column occupancy (0.074 H) and the band table's depth rows, which now match to 0.008 H at every band; the width rows carry the declared 8.0 m against the proxy's 6.95 m and are reported as the declared aspect.

A 6.0 x 1.5 m board with its back at z=0.25, 3 cm clear of the rail fronts at 0.22, its face 6 cm proud of the leg fronts, top at 6.55 with 0.3 m of rail showing above it - proxy rows 0.73-0.93 H. Held at 0.86 for the board width: the proxy fills 0.88 of its clear span and the plate's board is nearer 3.7:1, and at the declared 8 m span the build takes 4:1 with 0.4 m gaps rather than 0.9 m gaps the plate does not show.

Forest green field, white 0.04 m border rule 0.08 m in, Thai destination over its Latin transliteration left of centre with the distance at the right, and a chalky top-edge wash (#BDC6C5 over 2420 of 12000 bright px) fading within the top fifth, on a 4:1 atlas at one isotropic scale so the legend needs no anisotropy squash. The green ships lifted from the measured #2E644C to #347055 and the material records both the measurement and the 31-luma margin it now renders at.

Flange collars at 5.0 on both legs with rust on their undersides (#7B6757 over 313 rusty px) and a streak below; end-plate brackets at all four rail ends (#676562 with #806E5C rust); cap plates (#949392 with #826D5B rust); four gusset fins per foot (#656460). Held at 0.78 because the gussets are 0.10 m fins clamped by the declared 0.60 m depth where the proxy's plates are 0.9 m, and no bolt heads are modelled.

Eight staple rungs on the LEFT leg's OUTER (-x) face only, 0.5 to 3.65 m at 0.45 pitch, 0.20 m out with a 0.32 m crossbar - proxy columns 0-1 of 80, rows 0.06-0.52. Merged into the frame buffer: 288 triangles against the InstancedMesh draw call v1 spent on them. Nothing on the right leg.

Vertex ramp from the cap's #949392 through the averaged #7F8285 field to #5B5C5B plates and #7E6A57 foot rust, baked per part BEFORE the merge and carried through it (the shared concat drops color), multiplied under a seeded seamless 1 m spangle tile of 160 near-white blotches at 0.90-1.0 and seven faint run-off streaks. Rust is local to every bolted connection and thin, as the orange-filter counts say. Held at 0.84: the tile's mottle is a stand-in for hot-dip spangle, not a measurement of its scale.

review.critique: FINAL VERDICT. Overall visual fidelity 0.93 -- not a pass self-score. 780/16000 triangles, 10/12 draw calls, 8/8 materials, 10/16 unique geometries, 2 textures. The shopfront correction made the prop CHEAPER: deleting the invented door surround took its InstancedMesh with it, and folding the four intermediate mullions into the one system that remained left ten draw calls and ten geometries against eleven of each. review.critique: POST-SHIP CORRECTION 2 AND 3: THE LEGS WERE NOT JOINED TO THE BODY, AND THEN SHOWED A FLAT FACE. Both reported by eye, both then measured. Correction 2: the thigh root sat at y 0.205 while the body's surface at the thigh's own position is y 0.214 -- the bbox minimum of 0.1934 occurs at x=0 on the midline, and by 30 mm out the ellipsoid has curved back up, so boxes overlapped by 13.6 mm while surfaces grazed by 2.5. Correction 3: burying the root deeper left the tapered sweep's END CAP partly outside the body, a flat disc on a curved flank -- connected but visibly not joined. Removing the cap would leave a backfacing open rim (worse) and the taper rule forbids a root under 0.020, so instead the root moved INWARD and DEEPER to where the body can swallow it: sampling the body's own ellipsoids gives half-widths of 0.037 at y 0.228 but 0.040 at y 0.250, so the root rises to y 0.250 and moves in to x 0.010, and the sweep walks back out to x 0.030 as it descends. All 13 root-cap vertices now measure inside the body. THE MOST IMPORTANT FINDING WAS IN MY OWN INSTRUMENT. The new attachment checker used THREE.Raycaster for ray-parity point-in-mesh, and Raycaster honours the material's 'side' property, which is FrontSide -- so a ray leaving an interior point registers zero crossings and the test was exactly INVERTED, reporting inside as outside. It looked plausible because it still returned non-zero counts, and it had reported the beak joint as 4.6 mm. A control assertion caught it: the body's own centroid read as not inside the body. With DoubleSide the numbers are trustworthy, and the proof is that mirrored pairs now agree EXACTLY -- both thighs 45.3 mm, both wings 40.5 mm -- where before they differed 6.1 against 2.5. That control is now permanent and the script refuses to report if it fails. The corrected test then exposed a defect the broken one had hidden: beak-to-head was grazing at 0.4 mm, now 8.4 mm. The hock joint, marginal at 4.1 against 3.8 for a mirrored pair, is now 12.2 and 11.8. Every declared attachment measures at least 8.4 mm deep, and the gate suite gained an attachment-depth check that fails anything under 2 mm.

Every declared attachment now measures 8.4 mm deep or more, and mirrored pairs agree EXACTLY (both thighs 45.3 mm, both wings 40.5 mm), which is what proves the measurement sound.

assets.notes: subject is animal rather than prop, which selects the reconstruction profile with the chirality and swept-arc gates -- the landmark extractors are human-only, so animal does not run the anatomy track that character does.
